1. **The idea.** The animation compares buying a home with renting and investing the difference in stocks, using US history. A grid of tiles stands for different starting periods. A light tile means the buyer ended up ahead after ten years. A dark tile means the renter's stock pile was bigger. Frames 1–2 are labeled "2009 to mid-2016: nearly 4 in 5 lit." They also say "lit in stretches · one long dark stretch" and "after the crash: lit again." The footer says "US only · history, not a forecast," and a tag marks the whole thing as "ILLUSTRATIVE."

2. **What changes over time.** In frames 1–2 the grid shows the pattern across starting years. Light and dark tiles alternate, with one long dark block in the middle. In frames 3–6 a bar chart appears over the grid, titled "buyer ahead, pile in stocks, by length of stay." Its bars are added one at a time: 53.4% for 5 years, 49.5% for 10 years, and 21.9% for 15 years.

3. **What it means.** Neither option wins every time. Whether the buyer or the stock-investing renter comes out ahead depends on when you start and how long you stay. The buyer was ahead in about half of the historical 5-year and 10-year windows (53.4% and 49.5%). The buyer was ahead in only about a fifth of the 15-year windows (21.9%). So over longer stays, renting and investing the difference has usually come out ahead in this data. The long dark stretch shows that renting won for a whole run of starting years, not just scattered ones. The buyer's wins were also clustered in particular periods, such as the one after the crash.

4. **Advice a viewer would take.** The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would probably conclude that renting and investing the difference is not a sure win, since it is close to a coin flip at 5 to 10 years. They might also see that it has often won over long horizons. They would likely also see that timing matters and that past results don't predict the future.

5. **Source of that takeaway.** The text on screen suggests the "history, not a forecast" caution and the "it varies by period" point. The percentages and the pattern of tiles suggest the rest. The cautious reading in my answer to 4 is my own inference. The animation never tells the viewer what to do.
